sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01241v2 (arXiv:2601.01241v2 [cs.CR] 22 Jun 2026; abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01241; v1 also retrieved and compared, v3 does not exist)
statedGuarantee: SandScope executes portable tools under WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) or drives unmodified MCP servers over standard input/output (stdio), extracts LLM-visible sinks from tool results and prompt/message fields, and reports auditable source-to-sink witnesses from environment, file, and tool-input sources while separately recording network-intent and egress evidence. || Restated: this is a PRE-ADOPTION AUDIT framework, not a deployment-time enforcement layer. Two guarantees are bundled: (a) containment - on the portable path, an untrusted tool executed for audit is confined to an explicit WASI capability grant (env allowlist, one preopened directory, bounded stdout/stderr, network denied by default); (b) detection - any authority-bearing source byte that reaches an LLM-visible MCP field is reported as an auditable witness. Nothing is blocked in the deployed agent; the audited tool, once adopted, runs unmediated.
advertisedRhetoric: SandScope uses WASI as a containment backend for portable subjects. The WASI backend grants only selected environment variables, preopens a designated data directory, bounds captured standard output and standard error, and denies or mediates network behavior by default. || This gives the scanner an explicit capability interface for pre-adoption behavioral auditing. || Title rhetoric: “WASM-based Secure Execution and Runtime Analysis for MCP Tools”. Note the paper immediately tempers this itself: SandScope’s contribution is therefore not “WASM instead of OS sandboxing.”
tierSpan: This native path provides protocol fidelity but does not by itself provide the same containment guarantees as WASI. In practice, native scans of untrusted tools should be paired with an OS-level sandbox such as Docker or Bubblewrap
cheapestDefeat: Worked explicitly. GUARANTEE: (a) an audited tool cannot exceed the granted capability set; (b) authority-bearing bytes reaching an LLM-visible MCP field are reported. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: (a) the WASI runtime's capability grant; (b) the byte-level witness matcher (exact / separator-normalized / base64 / hex / ROT13 decoded) applied to sinks extracted from captured stdout and JSON-RPC transcripts. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: no sandbox escape is required for either. For (b), apply any transformation the matcher does not decode, or emit the value outside a region the sink extractor collects - the paper enumerates the gap itself: "SandScope does not infer arbitrary transformations, encrypted payloads, compressed payloads, hashes, semantic rewrites, summarized content, or flows where no recoverable source-derived bytes are exposed." A single AES call, a gzip, or a paraphrase by the tool defeats the whole detection layer while the flow still occurs. For (a), ship a tool that is not WASI-portable - by the paper's own account the ordinary case, since "The real-world corpus primarily uses the native MCP path for unmodified servers, while WASI is used when a portable artifact or shim is available." - whereupon it runs as an ordinary host subprocess with no containment at all and OS-level confinement is explicitly delegated to Docker/Bubblewrap OUTSIDE the system. TIER OF THE MECHANISM DEFEATED: a matcher over a captured output/protocol chokepoint, bypassed by any path that does not traverse it in recoverable form -> T3. CHARITABLE COUNTERWEIGHT (recorded for the adjudicator): considered ALONE, the WASI path is a genuine T2 bound - wasi_snapshot_preview1 exposes no process-spawn call and the host runtime refuses ungranted syscalls regardless of guest intent, so a WASI guest is bounded by the runtime, not by its own cooperation. The weakest-link rule nonetheless forces T3, because the guarantee as stated in the abstract spans BOTH execution paths and the native path - which carried most of the real-world evaluation - supplies no bound whatsoever.
placementSpan: Our primary adversary controls content or arguments that reach an otherwise benign or trusted-but-risky MCP tool. Such inputs include user prompts, LLM-generated tool arguments, retrieved web pages, GitHub issues, README files, API responses, and dependency metadata. || SECONDARY (A5, addressed but not tested): "Malicious or compromised MCP servers are a secondary supply-chain threat. They motivate contained execution during pre-adoption vetting, but SandScope’s runtime witness detection does not require the tool itself to be malicious."

coverageSpans.E1: WASI path bounds file access to one explicitly granted directory - "In the WASI path, this directory is preopened explicitly. In the native path, it is provided as a controlled workspace fixture." - and violations are recorded: "they provide execution evidence for actions such as blocked filesystem access, denied connections, or outbound-request attempts" PARTIAL: the preopen bounds the WASI guest (reads, writes, renames, unlinks) but the native stdio path gives the tool the auditor's own filesystem authority, and no write/rename/unlink mediation is described there.
coverageSpans.E2: PARTIAL. Provably bounded on one path, provably absent on the other. On the WASI path the capability interface is exhaustive ("The WASI backend grants only selected environment variables, preopens a designated data directory, bounds captured standard output and standard error, and denies or mediates network behavior by default.") and WASI exposes no spawn primitive, so neither a subprocess nor any descendant can exist. On the native stdio path the server is started as a host process and nothing in the paper mediates what it forks; process execution appears only as a PROFILING label, never as a control: "The current taxonomy includes network access, browser automation, cloud or SaaS operation, filesystem access, code repository operation, database access, credential or secret handling, shell or process execution, and unknown or benign utility." and "a semantic label is a declared capability rather than a vulnerability claim" DEPTH RULE: descendant spawns are unmediated on the native path -> ceiling is partial.
coverageSpans.E3: PARTIAL, and the covert-channel rule independently caps it there. The contract explicitly excludes the channel: "The current prototype does not claim complete network-flow mediation." and "We also do not fully mediate arbitrary network behavior in the current prototype; instead, we treat network-like patterns as signals and leave full network syscall instrumentation as future work." Charitable credit where earned: the WASI backend denies or mediates network behavior by default and denied connections are logged - "When an egress monitor or OS-level network policy is enabled, SandScope records denied connection attempts as host-and-port observations." Behavioral confirmation of the gap: the two false negatives in the controlled benchmark are exactly the egress cases - "The two false negatives occur in non-protocol C2-beacon subjects where the expected finding is an intent signal, but the emitted output does not produce a source-to-sink witness under the current extraction rules." Descendant egress is nowhere addressed.
coverageSpans.E4: PARTIAL, and this is the weakest cell in the coding - flagged for the adjudicator. The paper never names VCS push as a mediated effector. The charitable reading that supports 'partial' rather than 'not-covered' is purely derivative: a push requires network, and on the WASI path network is denied by default, so a WASI guest provably cannot push. Repository operations otherwise appear only as a declared-capability label ("code repository operation", in the taxonomy span quoted under E2), which is profiling, not mediation, and the native path is unbounded. A strict coder would score this not-covered.
coverageSpans.E5: NOT-COVERED, and worse than merely unaddressed - SandScope itself performs package installs on the auditor's host as part of scanning, and mediates none of it. Build is a first-class pipeline stage with its own failure column: "Build failures, startup or protocol-initialization failures, and call-timeout failures reflect packaging conventions, runtime dependencies, server entry-point discovery, credential requirements, and protocol behavior." (Table 3 reports 19 build failures across 91 resolved repositories.) The build necessarily precedes and sits outside the WASI sandbox, so third-party install hooks and their network activity execute with the auditor's full host authority. Nothing in the text mediates, observes, or even mentions install-hook behavior.
coverageSpans.E6: PARTIAL - capped by the published-credential-list rule. There is real mechanism: the WASI grant is an env-var allowlist (grants only selected environment variables), and credential exposure is actively probed with canaries: "SandScope seeds selected environment variables with unique canary values. These variables model secrets, tokens, user identifiers, local configuration, and private prompts that may be inherited by an MCP server from the host process." But the list is 'selected' and never enumerated, config files are not a modeled source, and keychain and cloud metadata endpoints are absent from the source taxonomy, which is fixed at four classes: environment, file, tool-input, network-like intent. Credential handling otherwise appears only as a declared-capability label. Undefined list -> cap at partial.
coverageSpans.E7: NOT-COVERED. Sub-agent spawn is not in the threat model, the source taxonomy, the sink taxonomy, or the capability taxonomy. The scope disclaimer confirms the agent loop is out of frame: "The prototype does not crawl the web, fuzz arbitrary arguments, or simulate a full multi-turn agent loop" Per the coding rules an unaddressed effector is not-covered, never not-applicable.

schneider.surrogate: A monitorable safety property, in two parts: (1) the WASI capability grant - a per-operation admissibility check a reference monitor can enforce on a prefix of the execution (env allowlist, single preopened directory, bounded output streams, network denied by default); and (2) a byte-level observation predicate - seeded canary bytes, or an exact / separator-normalized / base64 / hex / ROT13-decoded view of them, appear in an extracted LLM-visible sink region. Both are decidable on observed finite traces, which is exactly why the paper can report precision 1.000 with zero false positives.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is the non-monitorable one: absence of confused-deputy information flow from attacker-controlled external input to LLM-visible MCP fields - a confidentiality/information-flow hyperproperty over the set of executions, outside Schneider's EM-enforceable class. The paper is unusually explicit that it enforces the surrogate and not the objective: "SandScope is a positive-evidence detector, not a complete information-flow system" and "Absence of a witness therefore does not prove absence of a flow" This is a textbook split, and an honestly declared one.

notes:
VERSION. Coded against v2 (22 Jun 2026), the current version; v3 returns 404. v1 was retrieved and differs materially - it evaluates three representative tools and describes a three-stage pipeline, whereas v2 adds the 100-repository corpus, the evasion benchmark, the semantic profiling layer, and the native stdio path. Coding v1 would produce different coverage numbers but the same tier. Note also a naming split an adjudicator will trip over: the arXiv title is 'MCP-SandboxScan' while the system is called 'SandScope' throughout the body; the released code is at anonymous.4open.science under the MCP-SandboxScan name.

THE CORPUS QUESTION - IS WASI A GENUINE T2 BOUND? My answer: yes in kind, no in reach, and this paper is the best evidence in the corpus for that distinction. In kind, the WASI grant is genuinely T2-shaped and NOT a proxy: it binds what the guest process can do regardless of guest intent, it requires no cooperation from the guest, and it cannot be sidestepped by a subprocess that declines to call a hook - because wasi_snapshot_preview1 exposes no spawn primitive at all, so the T3-defeating move from the worked example is structurally unavailable. That is a stronger property than any in-process interposition and it deserves to be recorded as such. In reach, it fails on three counts, all of which the paper concedes rather than hides. (1) APPLICABILITY: WASI binds only code compiled to WASM or wrapped by a shim; every unmodified Node/Python/Go/Rust MCP server routes to the native stdio path with no containment, and that path carried the bulk of the real-world evaluation. (2) DELEGATION: the OS-level bound is explicitly outsourced to Docker or Bubblewrap, i.e. supplied by a composed system, not by this one - the paper says so in the sentence used as the tier span, and disclaims the framing directly in the advertisedRhetoric field. (3) LIFETIME: the bound exists only during the audit. Nothing is enforced at deployment time; the audited tool then runs in the real agent with full host authority. So for the SoK: WASI is a real capability boundary of T2 character, but in this system it is a scoped ANALYSIS boundary, not a DEPLOYMENT boundary - which is why the composite scores T3 under the weakest-link rule. The right T-12 sentence is that WASM isolation is neither 'neither OS nor proxy' nor a drop-in T2 substitute; it is a T2-grade bound whose applicability domain (portable artifacts only) is far narrower than the effector surface it is asked to cover.

CATEGORY CAVEAT FOR THE ADJUDICATOR. This paper is a scanner, not a runtime. Applying an enforcement-tier rubric to it risks a category error in the unfavorable direction: SandScope does not claim to stop E1-E7 in a live agent and should not be read as failing at something it never attempted. Every 'partial' above should be read as 'partial DURING AUDIT, on the portable path'; the deployment-time coverage of all seven effectors is nil by design. If the SoK has a bucket for pre-adoption vetting tools distinct from runtime enforcement layers, this belongs there, and its tier should be reported with that qualifier attached.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN. (i) E4 is the softest cell - I scored partial on the derivative argument that a push needs network and WASI denies network by default; a strict coder would say the paper never addresses VCS at all and score not-covered. I would not contest that revision. (ii) EVIDENCE GRADE sits on the L2/L3 boundary. I assigned L2 for the behavioral confirmation (30 controlled cross-language subjects with TP/FN/FP/TN, an evasion benchmark, 91 resolved repositories, 35 dynamically scanned, 33 re-executed, 12 with witnesses). The case for L3 is that the authors publish reproducible bypasses of their own detector - the two C2-beacon false negatives, plus Table 2's demonstration that raw matching fails on ROT13/hex/base64/chunked - and release the code. I stayed at L2 because those are self-reported recall limits inside their own fixtures rather than an independent bypass of a claimed guarantee; a human may reasonably move it to L3. (iii) ADVERTISED TIER: I recorded T2 on the strength of the title and the WASI containment language, but this paper advertises unusually conservatively and the gap between advertised and scored here reflects path applicability rather than overclaiming. Among corpus papers this is one of the least rhetorically inflated; the T2->T3 drop should not be read as a dishonesty finding.

E5 IS THE UNDER-DISCUSSED FINDING. The scanner runs a build step on 91 untrusted third-party repositories on the auditor's host, outside any sandbox, before the WASI sandbox is ever entered. Install hooks and their network activity are unmediated and unobserved. A malicious MCP repository - precisely the secondary adversary the paper names - compromises the auditor at install time and never reaches the sandbox at all. The paper's own honest note that native scans should be paired with Docker or Bubblewrap applies with more force to the build stage than to the execution stage, and is not made there.
